notes:
Tasks work the way people actually hand work over now.

A task you have been given sits in To Do until you answer it. Press Accept and it starts — there is no second button to find, because agreeing to do something and starting it are the same moment. Decline instead and you say why, so whoever set it can give it to somebody else rather than wonder.

As you go, you say how far along you are. Drag the bar or tap 25, 50, 75, 100. Nobody can see your progress unless you put it there, and nothing guesses it from the calendar.

Finishing is now handing in rather than closing. You press Submit and say what you did; it goes to whoever gave you the job, and they either approve it or send it back with a note saying what still needs doing. Sent back, it reopens with everything you have already written, attached and recorded still on it — you are not starting again. If a task does not need checking, whoever sets it can turn the review off.

A task too big for one person can be split into pieces, and each piece is a real task of its own with its own owner, deadline and share of the points. The points come out of the task rather than being invented: hand out all of them and you keep none, hand out sixty of a hundred and the forty left are yours. They divide equally unless you change them, and the form shows what is left as you type. Leave a piece unassigned and it is offered to your team instead of given to anybody — the first person to pick it up gets it.

Two different things you could only do clumsily before now have their own buttons. Delegate hands the work down, and from then on you are the one who approves it — so a director who asked a manager for a report is not made to read the junior's first draft. Transfer is the other one, and it is for a task that reached the wrong person: it moves across completely, resets to To Do, and you stop hearing about it. The app says plainly which one you are doing before it does it.

If a deadline is not going to happen, say so instead of missing it. Ask for more time, pick the date and give a reason; the person who set the task grants it or refuses it, and either way you are told. The work carries on while you wait.

Every task now carries its urgency in its colour — red for urgent, amber for medium, grey for low — and turns green when it is done. Something past its deadline is marked late without being repainted, so a low-priority job that has slipped still reads as low priority. And whether you delivered on time is now decided by when you HANDED IT IN, not by when somebody got round to approving it.

The list counts what matters at a glance — how many are yours, late, waiting, in review and finished — and each figure is a filter. Sort by deadline, by the day it was given to you, by how long it has been sitting there, by points or by urgency. Open one and you get the whole thing: the details, the pieces, and one conversation.

That conversation is the other fix. Everything anybody said about a task is now in one place — the remark you wrote when you handed it in, the manager's note when they sent it back, and the ordinary comments in between, from the person it is assigned to and the person who assigned it both. They used to be scattered across a history nobody opened.

A task that fails to open no longer throws you back to the list. It stays put, says what went wrong, and offers to try again.
